content: At the last CS meeting we discussed pushing this so that complexity work can proceed while we wait for more ways of formalising TMs, so status updates are welcome. :)
Sorry, this one is my fault. I have not had time to review it yet. I will give it a thorough review before the next meeting.

Relevant question here : have we decided on using an inductive type of possible moves on a TM? If so this PR needs to be updated to that definition. I personally recommend it because it lets us write Prog/FreeM programs on TMs easily and without touching their underlying config. This last part is important since we need to ensure that TMs are not using any knowledge of the tape index of the head (which would be part of the config) in the description of their transitions.
Otherwise we inadvertently end up with an infinite state TM.

Can you sketch what you mean by that? I think it could be useful later on by defining a multi-tape TM "on top of" a computation model with attached resource model so we can capture sub-linear space and still have a "usable" computation model. But I'm not sure if we are talking about the same thing or not.
I think it is orthgonal, since I am describing how the transition function should be written.

Essentially there are two views of the transition function of a TM.

  1. In the textbook view, in a single step, a machine performs, a read, write, and move, and Fabrizio's NDTM captures this textbook style definition.
  2. The moves of a TM are defined by an inductive type (similar to my query types). A move is either a read, write, updateState, or move constructor with suitable arguments. This is a more basic list of operations than arbitrary single step transition functions, but any transition function can be built from them. This version is much easier to use to build TMs using lean functions, because you have a small number of basic operations.

So you are saying that splitting the step into individual operations make it easier to build TMs? In my opinion, it is easier to build TMs when one step allows to read, write and move at the same time because otherwise, you have to store the read symbol in the state. Furthermore, if you split the step, you can still use the "combined step" model, but the converse is harder (i.e. storing the read symbols in the state).

We already talked about it: If you store the read symbol "outside" the computational model, you get into a lot more problems.

Thanks! I will add references and also some discussion about why it was modeled like that, and I think I will also switch to functions instead of BiTape, it makes more sense when we have to track the position of the tape heads anyway.

Thanks for all the comments so far! I extended the design discussion, changed from BiTape to ℤ → Option Symbol, added explicit tape head position tracking (we need that anyway to determine the space usage) and made the step function total (it becomes inert on a halting configuration).
Also I made the "ComputesInTimeAndSpace" a bit more flexible than what we have in e.g. single tape TM: It takes an embedding from another input/output alphabet. This allows us to talk about the time and space requirement of a function List Bool → List Bool and thus compare different models to each other.

So the standard presentation of a TM indeed has a single step transition that reads, writes, and moves in a single step. If you write programs at this level of granularity then you have to write the single step transition function (which is basically an if-then-else statement, that performs a single step) and then reason about the effect of extending it. I claim that this is a big reason why TMs are inconvenient to write, because this single step amounts to a large number of basic operations. So the single step semantics (make a config transition according to this strange table) is very inconvenient. Extending it to what an execution of the TM on a given input does is also painful.

Instead an inductive type that specifies the five moves that a TM can perform explicitly makes writing TM programs and reasoning about them simpler since your small step semantics for the TM only has one of 5 possible cases. Note that I am explicitly drawing inspiration from my "all models are query models" approach.

At the risk of quoting my library, I claim that writing programs with this approach is easier than writing programs with arbitrary single step transitions that combine read,write, and move in one step :

The basic operations of a single tape TM

To adapt this to a multi-tape TM, one simply adds tape indices to the operations that need it. 

inductive Dir where
  | Left
  | Right
  | Stop

/--
A query type of possible operating steps in a Turing machine.
-/
inductive TMQuery : (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) → Type → Type where
  /-- Read a symbol under the TM head on the tape -/
  | readTape {tm} (inpCfg : tm.Cfg) : TMQuery tm (Option Symbol)
  /-- Read the state of the TM -/
  | readState {tm} (inpCfg : tm.Cfg) : TMQuery tm (Option tm.State)
  /-- Write a symbol under the TM head on the tape -/
  | write {tm} (inpCfg : tm.Cfg) (s : Option Symbol) : TMQuery tm tm.Cfg
  /-- Update the TM's state -/
  | update {tm} (inpCfg : tm.Cfg) (st : tm.State): TMQuery tm tm.Cfg
  /-- Move the TM one step in the specified direction or stay in place -/
  | move {tm} (inpCfg : tm.Cfg) (dir : Dir) : TMQuery tm tm.Cfg

Note that I don't claim that the above mentioned code is the final answer to this conundrum. I am working on something called stateful models that will allow us to discard the tm.Cfg parameter to all constructors. Concretely instead of lowering FreeM programs to the Id monad, we lower them to a state monad and make the configuration of the TM part of the state of the monad.

More input on space complexity : the Papadimitriou defintion seems to be the preferred choice.
One expert says DSPACE(loglog n) = DSPACE(1) would also hold for the papadimitriou defintion.

This is not true. Exercise 2.8.11(d) on page 54 shows that DSPACE(1)=REG, exercises 2.8.11(f+g) on page 55 construct a non-regular language in log log n. And exercise 2.8.12 shows that DSPACE(o(log log n))=DSPACE(1)
I would like to work on these extremely elementary results next, but for this we have to use the correct definition of space.
Correction, I should have said DSPACE(o(log log n)) = DSPACE(O(1))

and this holds for both papadimitriou and Barak-Arora machines, The machines considered DSPACE(o(log log n)) in the Barak-Arora book would also be DSPACE (o(log log n)) in the Papadimitriou definition.

Ok, good. Exercise 1 of chapter 4.4 in the draft version of Arora-Barak is about proving that DSPACE(1)=DSPACE(log log n). So this is all consistent with my note in the PR that you get non-regular languages in constant space if you only count the cells that were non-empty during the computation.
I think that might be a typo for the same reason I stated above.

Either way we had some long discussions and the conclusion is that the Barak-Arora definition is broken because with it, one can simulate counter machines with O(1) space, and counter machines are Turing complete with 3 or more counters. Consensus : let's follow Papadimitriou's definition.

I finally found time to update the pr. Among other things, I changed Symbol and State from Type* to Type because I understood a comment by @Eric Wieser such that if both are Fintype then allowing other universes is not really helpful anyway. Would be great to get a confirmation of that assumption. Thanks!
You could just move the finiteness assumptions to section variables where needed, I guess? Or is there a reason to keep them? We typically don't bundle those.

As long as the variables are not explicit, they are section variables. I guess I could also make them explicit section variables. But I think this is a separate issue isn’t it? The variables will likely always be Fintype and the question was if it makes sense to use Tyoe* in that case. Or did I misunderstand you?
Or are you talking about the bundling of State? The point there is that the state type really should not matter to the outside, but I guess i could still pull it up.

I would unbundle State and not have assumptions on finiteness in the definition of TM like [stateFintype : Fintype State] at all.
It might give us hassles if/when we prove that a multi-tape TM is as powerful as a single-tape NTM or even a deterministic automaton (where symbols and states are in Type*).

Re 'likely always be Fintype': in computability studies, probably. I wonder if we'll ever use a TM or similar to formalise a tracer, a monitor, or something like that. In that case, all finiteness assumptions should be off as both states and symbols would be from infinite types (whose elements would be finite though, so space used etc. would still be finite). I don't actually know at this point yet, so I'd err on generality if it doesn't hurt the specific development at hand outside of making assumptions explicit with variables or parameters here and there.

Yeah it probably makes sense to keep the structures and other definitions as general as possible and only restrict to finiteness for the „f is computable in t time and s space in the k-tape TM model of complexity“-definition

Ok, I just updated the PR, please take a look. I removed the Fintype requirement entirely, removed the bundling of State and decoupled Cfg from tm. For the "ComputableInTimeAndSpace", the TM is existentially qualified and instead of saying "there exist State and Symbol that are Fintype" I just went for Fin state and Fin symbol, because that way we don't have to talk about class instances and the actual type does not really matter in the statement of that Prop. Once we start using ComputableInTimeAndSpace, we can add a lemmas that can relate TMs with different symbol and state sets (also useful for extending TMs to larger state sets / larger alphabets, etc).

One more change: I unbundled the input from the configuration, that way the type system ensures that the input "stays the same" across steps and it is also clearer what is "stored" in the machine, i.e. what is part of a configuration.
